claim: The perceptual space for human color vision has three dimensions.
source: The perceptual space for human color vision has three dimensions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about color vision, supported by historical experimental evidence mentioned in the text.

claim: Experimental proof that color vision has three dimensions dates to the 17th century.
source: Experimental proof of this dates to the 17th century, when it was found that every color sensation can be matched by mixing together three primary lights, but not if only two lights are available (Mollon, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mollon, 2003.

claim: Every color sensation can be matched by mixing together three primary lights, but not if only two lights are available.
source: it was found that every color sensation can be matched by mixing together three primary lights, but not if only two lights are available (Mollon, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mollon, 2003.

claim: Every color sensation can be fully characterized by three numbers, namely the intensity of the primaries that match it.
source: Therefore every color sensation can be fully characterized by three numbers, namely the intensity of the primaries that match it.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the three-primary mixing result.

claim: Color vision is based on three kinds of cone photoreceptors in the retina that differ in their sensitivity to the wavelength spectrum of light.
source: We now know that color vision is based on three kinds of cone photoreceptors in the retina that differ in their sensitivity to the wavelength spectrum of light.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the biological basis of color vision.

claim: Any pattern of excitation among cones can be matched by an appropriate mix of three primary lights.
source: Any pattern of excitation among cones can be matched by an appropriate mix of three primary lights, and this is the basis for RGB color display devices.
evidence: This is established knowledge about color vision and display technology.

claim: Human subjects can distinguish about 1–2 million different colors.
source: in practice human subjects can distinguish about 1–2 million different colors (Masaoka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Masaoka et al., 2013.

claim: Humans have approximately 400 types of olfactory receptors.
source: Human olfaction begins with the binding of odor molecules to olfactory receptors, of which there exist ∼400 types (Malnic et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Malnic et al., 2004.

claim: All olfactory receptor types differ in their relative sensitivity to various odorants.
source: It is believed that these receptor types all differ in their relative sensitivity to various odorants.
evidence: This is stated as a belief, indicating it is based on current scientific understanding.

claim: Two odors can only be distinguished if they cause different patterns of activity among receptor types.
source: Two odors can only be distinguished if they cause different patterns of activity among these types.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the understanding of sensory discrimination.

claim: The neural space of odors at the input to the olfactory system has 400 dimensions.
source: Thus the neural space of odors at the very input to the olfactory system would seem to have 400 dimensions, many more than encountered in the color system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the number of receptor types.

claim: The space of odors is dominated by just one or two dimensions based on perceptual similarities analysis.
source: from a quantitative analysis of perceptual similarities it has been argued that the space of odors is dominated by just one or two dimensions (Secundo et al., 2014), much fewer than the 400 dimensions at the level of sensory receptors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Secundo et al., 2014.

claim: The number of discriminable odors is thought to be only 10,000.
source: Similarly the number of discriminable odors is thought to be only 10,000, although this estimate is largely anecdotal (Gilbert, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilbert, 2008, though noted as anecdotal.

claim: Bushdid et al. (2014) claimed that humans can discriminate one trillion odors.
source: a recent article claims that 'Humans can discriminate one trillion odors' (Bushdid et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct citation of the claim from Bushdid et al., 2014.

claim: The claim that humans can discriminate one trillion odors was based on experiments where humans discriminated successfully only 148 pairs of odors.
source: Remarkably, these claims were based on an experimental study in which humans discriminated successfully only 148 pairs of odors.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data from Bushdid et al., 2014.

claim: The mathematical method used by Bushdid et al. to extrapolate from 148 discriminated odor pairs to trillions fails.
source: Here I show that this mathematical method fails, and as a result the claims are without any basis.
evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript, supported by the analyses presented.

claim: The data on human olfaction are equally consistent with a trillion discriminable odors and with just 10.
source: We will see that the data on human olfaction are equally consistent with a trillion discriminable odors and with just 10 (and anything in between).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the analyses in the manuscript.

claim: If the same method were applied to human color vision, one would conclude that humans can distinguish at least 10^27 colors.
source: Moreover, if the same method were applied to human color vision, one would conclude that humans can distinguish at least 1027 colors, in dramatic conflict with experimental evidence.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation in the manuscript.

claim: Bushdid et al. made mixtures by drawing a number (N) of primary odors from 128 substances and mixing those in equal parts.
source: From these primary odors the authors made mixtures by drawing a number (N) of primary odors and mixing those in equal parts.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure from Bushdid et al., 2014.

claim: Bushdid et al. assumed that the ability of humans to discriminate two odors improves systematically with the distance between mixtures.
source: The authors assume that the ability of humans to discriminate two odors improves systematically with this distance.
evidence: This describes an assumption in the Bushdid et al. analysis.

claim: Bushdid et al. found that the probability of discrimination increases with the number of unshared components M.
source: Indeed they find that the probability of discrimination increases with M (Figure 3B of Bushdid et al., 2014).
evidence: This references data from Bushdid et al., 2014.

claim: Bushdid et al. defined the critical distance D as the separation M at which 50% of mixture pairs are discriminable.
source: They define the critical distance D as that separation M at which 50% of the mixture pairs are discriminable.
evidence: This describes the definition used in Bushdid et al., 2014.

claim: A toy microbe model with three response states ('yuck', 'yum', 'meh') yields an estimate of approximately 9×10^11 discriminable odors using the Bushdid et al. method.
source: This leads to an estimate of ∼9·1011 discriminable odors (Figure 1B,C, see Figure 3D of Bushdid et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The toy microbe model recognizes only three classes of odors by construction.
source: Yet we know by construction that it recognizes only three classes of odors.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the model construction.

claim: At most three odors can be produced such that each can be discriminated from all the others in the toy microbe model.
source: Thus one can produce at most three odors such that each can be discriminated from all the others.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the three-state nature of the model.

claim: The space of all colored lights has infinite dimensions.
source: The space of all colored lights has infinite dimensions.
evidence: This is based on the fact that light spectra are continuous functions.

claim: Each light is characterized by its wavelength spectrum S(λ), which specifies how much power exists at each wavelength λ.
source: Each light is characterized by its wavelength spectrum S(λ), which specifies how much power exists at each wavelength λ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the physical characterization of light.

claim: The sensory space of human color vision has only 3 dimensions.
source: However, as introduced above, the sensory space of human color vision has only 3 dimensions (Wandell, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wandell, 1995.

claim: For each cone type in the retina, the excitation is determined by the rate of photon absorption by its visual pigment.
source: For each of the three cone types in the retina, the excitation is determined by the rate of photon absorption by its visual pigment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cone photoreceptor function.

claim: The photon absorption rate is a linear function of the spectrum of the light.
source: In turn, that rate is a linear function of the spectrum of the light, namely the projection of the light spectrum onto the absorption spectrum of the pigment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor physics.

claim: When two lights are mixed together, the resulting cone excitation is the sum of the effects of the individual lights.
source: If two lights are mixed together, the resulting excitation is the sum of the effects of the individual lights.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the linearity of light mixing in color vision.

claim: Human color vision begins by projecting the infinite space of lights down onto a subspace of just 3 dimensions.
source: Therefore human color vision begins by projecting the infinite space of lights down onto a subspace of just 3 dimensions, spanned by the three cone excitations.
evidence: This is an inference from the properties of cone photoreceptors.

claim: There are upward of 1 million discriminable lights in human color vision.
source: By systematic probing of the 3-dimensional space one finds there are upward of 1 million discriminable lights, in the sense that any two of them will look different in a pairwise comparison (Masaoka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Masaoka et al., 2013.

claim: In the color vision simulation, a difference of 0.01 along any dimension is discriminable.
source: The level of noise is chosen so that a difference of 0.01 along any dimension is discriminable, which gives 1 million discriminable vectors in the unit cube.
evidence: This is a parameter choice in the simulation described in the manuscript.

claim: In the color vision simulation, all 30-light mixtures are discriminable if they differ by as little as one component.
source: From this simulation, I find that all 30-light mixtures are discriminable if they differ by as little as one component (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Each primary light in the color simulation has a vector length of 1/30.
source: Each of the primary lights has a vector length of 1/30 (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the simulation setup.

claim: A single unshared component can separate two mixture vectors by more than 1/30 in the RGB space.
source: This means that a single unshared component can separate the two mixture vectors by more than 1/30 in the RGB space.
evidence: This is an inference from the vector length of primary lights.

claim: The critical distance D = 1 in the color vision simulation.
source: So the critical distance D = 1.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation.

claim: Using the Bushdid et al. method on color vision yields more than 10^27 discriminable colors in the 128-dimensional space.
source: From this one calculates there are more than 1027 discriminable colors in the 128-dimensional space probed here (Figure 1C, see Figures 3D and S1B of Bushdid et al., 2014).
evidence: This is calculated using the Bushdid et al. formula on the simulation results.

claim: The methods of Bushdid et al. would conclude that humans can discriminate an infinite number of colors when not limiting the starting space to 128 primary lights.
source: Thus the methods of Bushdid et al. (2014) would conclude that humans can discriminate an infinite number of colors.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation with infinite dimensionality.

claim: The analysis method of Bushdid et al. fails the 'positive control test' when applied to color vision.
source: We can conclude that the analysis method fails the 'positive control test', namely the application to a related problem with known solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the color vision simulation results.

claim: The human odor discrimination data in Bushdid et al. could be explained by as few as 10 odor percepts.
source: Given that the analysis of Bushdid et al. can vastly overestimate the number of discriminable stimuli, one wonders whether the human odor discrimination data in that report could equally be explained by a much smaller number of odor percepts. That is indeed the case.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the ring model simulation.

claim: A one-dimensional ring model with Gaussian noise of 0.4 radians fits the Bushdid et al. data well.
source: With a noise value of 0.4 (SD of the Gaussian noise measured in radians) the fit to the data is quite good. Almost all the data points are within the 1 SD error bars.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C comparing model to data.

claim: For a noise value of 0.4, at most 10 vectors can be placed around the unit circle such that each is discriminable from its neighbors.
source: For a noise value of 0.4, how many mutually discriminable stimuli are there? We should use the standard of Bushdid et al. (2014) for discriminability of an odor pair: 50% correct identification in the 'odd-man-out' odor test. With that criterion, one can place at most 10 vectors around the unit circle such that each is discriminable from its neighbors.
evidence: This is calculated from the ring model with the specified noise level.

claim: The published measurements are consistent with a model in which humans can distinguish just 10 olfactory stimuli from each other.
source: Therefore, the published measurements are consistent with a model in which humans can distinguish just 10 olfactory stimuli from each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ring model analysis.

claim: The experiments in Bushdid et al. did not come close to exploring the richness of human olfactory experience.
source: Many of us have experienced more than 10 different smells, so these experiments did not come close to exploring the richness of human olfactory experience.
evidence: This is an inference based on common experience and the analysis results.

claim: To confirm that 10 odors are mutually discriminable by brute force, one has to compare each odor to every other one.
source: To confirm that 10 odors are mutually discriminable by brute force one has to compare each odor to every other one.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the requirements for exhaustive discrimination testing.

claim: Bushdid et al. did 260 pairwise comparisons, of which only about half were discriminable.
source: The authors did 260 pairwise comparisons, of which only about half were discriminable.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Bushdid et al. experiments.

claim: If one allows for higher numbers of dimensions in odor space, the predicted number of discriminable odors increases approximately exponentially with the dimensionality.
source: If one allows for higher numbers of dimensions, then the predicted number of discriminable odors increases, approximately exponentially with the dimensionality of the perceptual space (L Abbott, E Schaffer, and R Axel, personal communication).
evidence: This is based on personal communication with other researchers.

claim: The results of Bushdid et al. are equally consistent with 10 or a trillion discriminable odors or anything in between.
source: Since we do not know the dimensionality of odor space, the results of Bushdid et al. (2014) are equally consistent with 10 or a trillion discriminable odors or anything in between.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis showing the method's inability to distinguish hypotheses.

claim: The experiments in Bushdid et al. fail to distinguish alternative hypotheses for the number of discriminable odors.
source: In other words, the experiments fail to distinguish alternative hypotheses for the number of discriminable odors, even absurd ones that are clearly incorrect.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The failure of the Bushdid et al. method occurs in the implicit assignment of odor percepts to different spheres in stimulus space.
source: The failure of the method in Bushdid et al. (2014) occurs after the sphere-packing estimate (Figure 1B). It involves a step that is never mentioned but implicit in the procedure: the assignment of odor percepts to the different spheres in stimulus space.
evidence: This is an analysis of where the method fails.

claim: Bushdid et al. assume that every one of the spheres packed into the space corresponds to a different odor percept.
source: First, the authors assume that every one of the spheres packed into the space corresponds to a different odor percept. But this is unwarranted.
evidence: This is an analysis of an implicit assumption in the Bushdid et al. method.

claim: The measurement of critical distance for discrimination only ensures that neighboring spheres correspond to different percepts.
source: The measurement of critical distance for discrimination only ensures that neighboring spheres correspond to different percepts, it says nothing about more distant spheres.
evidence: This is a logical analysis of what the critical distance measurement implies.

claim: The same odor percept may recur over and over again for physically distinct odor mixtures.
source: Thus the same odor percept may recur over and over again for physically distinct odor mixtures.
evidence: This is a logical possibility that violates the Bushdid et al. assumption.

claim: Three colors are sufficient to color close-packed pennies in 2D so that no adjacent ones have the same color.
source: In fact, three colors are sufficient (Figure 4B), so just three percepts could account for an infinite number of spheres in a 2-dimensional odor space.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B and is a known result from graph theory.

claim: If the percept depends only on a single function of the coordinates, odors become more discriminable with distance along one dimension but remain indiscriminable along all other dimensions.
source: Here I showed that there is a simple and natural way to violate that assumption, namely if the percept depends only on a single function of the coordinates. Then the odors become more discriminable with distance along one dimension, but remain indiscriminable along all other dimensions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the penny coloring example in Figure 4C.

claim: If percepts live in some low-dimensional space embedded in 128 dimensions, this produces efficient labeling of close-packed spheres.
source: More generally, if the percepts live in some low-dimensional space (as is the case, e.g., for color vision and for the hearing of pure tones) and then one embeds that space in 128 dimensions, this will produce a similarly efficient labeling of the close-packed spheres.
evidence: This is a generalization from the specific examples analyzed.

claim: The definition of critical distance D as 50% discriminability is a weakness of the Bushdid et al. method.
source: This brings us to a second weakness of the method: the definition of the critical distance D. This is taken as the distance at which 50% of odor mixture pairs are discriminable.
evidence: This is an analysis of a methodological weakness.

claim: Two points separated by D in odor space only need to produce a different percept 50% of the time according to the Bushdid et al. definition.
source: In other words, two points separated by D in odor space only need to produce a different percept 50% of the time.
evidence: This is a restatement of the Bushdid et al. definition of critical distance.

claim: Just two colors (white and black) can paint alternating spheres such that every sphere is different from 50% of its neighbors.
source: That can be done trivially with just two colors, painting alternating spheres white and black. That makes every sphere different from 50% of all its neighbors.
evidence: This is a logical demonstration of how the 50% criterion can be satisfied with minimal percepts.

claim: To ensure that a sphere-coloring system uses at least 10,000 odors, one would need to raise the criterion for discriminability to 99.99%.
source: A popular estimate for the number of discriminable odors (though without solid scientific basis, as reviewed in Bushdid et al., 2014) is around 10,000. To ensure that a sphere-coloring system uses at least 10,000 odors, one would need to raise the criterion for discriminability in the definition of D to 99.99%.
evidence: This is a calculation based on graph coloring requirements.

claim: The mathematical method for exploring sensory spaces advocated in Bushdid et al. does not work.
source: The arguments above illustrate that the mathematical method for exploring sensory spaces advocated in Bushdid et al. (2014) does not work.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by multiple analyses.

claim: The extrapolation in Bushdid et al. presumes that the space of odor percepts has at least 128 dimensions.
source: Fundamentally the extrapolation presumes that the space of odor percepts has at least 128 dimensions.
evidence: This is an analysis of an implicit assumption in the Bushdid et al. method.

claim: The 128 primary odors chosen in Bushdid et al. must represent 'orthogonal' directions in perceptual space for their method to work.
source: Furthermore, the 128 primary odors chosen must represent 'orthogonal' directions in that space, so that the percept varies with distance in the same manner and independently along each of these dimensions.
evidence: This is an analysis of what assumptions are required for the Bushdid et al. method to be valid.

claim: Violation of the high-dimensionality assumption leads to dramatic failure of the estimate in Bushdid et al.
source: Violation of those assumptions, for example if the true dimensionality of odor space is much less than 128, leads to dramatic failure of the estimate.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulations in the manuscript.

claim: Classic studies of color vision obtained the number of discriminable colors (approximately 1 million) without doing n^2 discrimination tests.
source: Classic studies of color vision and tone hearing have achieved that. For color vision, the answer is approximately n = 1 million. How can one come to that conclusion without doing n2 discrimination tests?
evidence: This is a statement about how classic color vision studies were conducted.

claim: Success in counting discriminable stimuli is possible by taking advantage of the systematic structure of the perceptual space.
source: This is possible only by taking advantage of the systematic structure of the perceptual space.
evidence: This is an explanation of how classic discrimination studies achieved efficiency.

claim: Transitivity of discrimination applies in color vision and tone hearing.
source: For example, if light A looks more red than light B and B looks more red than C, then one can trust that A will look more red than C. The same applies in tone hearing: If tone A sounds lower than tone B, and B sounds lower than C, then A will sound lower than C.
evidence: This is established knowledge about perceptual discrimination.

claim: Transitivity of discrimination reduces the experimental burden from order(n^2) down to order(n).
source: This transitivity of discrimination means that it is sufficient to measure discrimination of neighboring stimuli to ensure mutual discrimination of all stimuli in the set, which reduces the experimental burden from order(n2) down to order(n).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of transitivity.

claim: Success of percept-counting studies relied on recognizing that the perceptual space is low-dimensional.
source: So success of these percept-counting studies relied entirely on recognizing early on that the perceptual space is low-dimensional.
evidence: This is an analysis of why classic studies succeeded.

claim: One needs to first answer 'how many dimensions span the perceptual space of odors' to properly study olfaction.
source: How to apply those insights to olfaction? Clearly one needs to first answer 'how many dimensions span the perceptual space of odors'?
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: The number of 400 human odorant receptor types sets an upper bound on the dimensionality of the perceptual space.
source: The number of 400 human odorant receptor types certainly sets an upper bound on the dimensionality of the perceptual space.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the structure of the sensory system.

claim: We may need many receptors simply to sense the molecules of interest, not to disambiguate all possible mixtures of those molecules.
source: However, there may be another explanation: We need this many receptors simply to sense the molecules of interest, not to disambiguate all possible mixtures of those molecules.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in the manuscript.

claim: E. coli has five different chemoreceptor proteins with different ligand spectra.
source: The bacterium Escherichia coli illustrates this idea: It has five different chemoreceptor proteins with different ligand spectra.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli chemotaxis.

claim: The outputs of all five E. coli receptors converge on a single variable, the concentration of the CheY signaling molecule.
source: The outputs of all five receptors readily converge on a single variable, namely the concentration of the CheY signaling molecule (Grebe and Stock, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grebe and Stock, 1998.

claim: E. coli projects the 5-dimensional receptor space onto a 1-dimensional perceptual space of attraction/repulsion.
source: E. coli projects the 5-dimensional receptor space onto a 1-dimensional perceptual space of attraction/repulsion.
evidence: This is an inference from the convergence onto CheY concentration.

claim: It is difficult to make a generic amino acid receptor with high sensitivity.
source: Presumably it is difficult to make a generic amino acid receptor with high sensitivity.
evidence: This is speculation about molecular constraints on receptor design.

claim: Odorants in the human nose are present at micromolar concentrations or less, in a mucus soup of other components at millimolar concentration.
source: The molecules of interest are there at micromolar concentrations or less, in a mucus soup of other components at millimolar concentration.
evidence: This is knowledge about the chemical environment in the nose.

claim: To sense odorants separately from mucus, a receptor needs to bind them with high affinity.
source: To sense the odorants separately from the mucus, a receptor needs to bind them with high affinity.
evidence: This is an inference from the concentration differences.

claim: High affinity binding means many contact sites between binding pocket and ligand, which leads to selectivity for the shape of the ligand.
source: That means many contact sites between binding pocket and ligand, which in turn leads to selectivity for the shape of the ligand.
evidence: This is knowledge about molecular binding principles.

claim: Even if the olfactory system just wanted to distinguish odors along one dimension, it would be impossible to make a receptor that is selective just for the attractants.
source: Even if the olfactory system just wanted to distinguish odors along one dimension (attractive/repulsive), it would be impossible to make a receptor that is selective just for the attractants.
evidence: This is speculation about constraints on receptor design.

claim: Nature makes many receptors that are each selective for small groups of related molecules and then combines their signals using the nervous system.
source: Instead Nature makes many receptors that are each selective for small groups of related molecules and then combines their signals appropriately using the nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference about how the olfactory system is organized.

claim: The dimensionality of receptor space is determined by molecular principles involving the number of ligands, their concentrations, binding energetics, and protein design limitations.
source: In this picture the dimensionality of receptor space is determined by molecular principles involving the number of ligands of interest, their relevant concentrations, the energetics of ligand binding, and the design limitations of protein structures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about what determines receptor space dimensionality.

claim: The dimensionality of perceptual space is governed by behavioral and ecological constraints.
source: The dimensionality of perceptual space, on the other hand, is governed by behavioral and ecological constraints: the nature of olfactory cues in the environment, the kinds of decisions the animal makes based on odorants, and the need to associate new odors with unusual events.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about what determines perceptual space dimensionality.

claim: There is no principled reason that perceptual space should have the same dimensionality as receptor space.
source: There is no principled reason that this perceptual space should have the same dimensionality as the receptor space.
evidence: This is a logical argument based on the different constraints on each space.

claim: Every hair follicle on human skin contains a sensitive mechanoreceptor, several million altogether.
source: Every hair follicle on our skin contains a sensitive mechanoreceptor, several million altogether (Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zimmerman et al., 2014.

claim: Humans can reliably detect the bending of an individual hair almost anywhere on the body.
source: This makes us highly sensitive to touch: we can reliably detect the bending of an individual hair almost anywhere on the body.
evidence: This is knowledge about human touch sensitivity.

claim: Humans cannot discriminate all patterns of bent hairs.
source: But clearly we cannot discriminate all patterns of bent hairs.
evidence: This is based on common experience.

claim: Brushing across your head twice in a row feels very much the same, even though it causes two different patterns of activity among touch receptors.
source: Brushing across your head twice in a row feels very much the same, even though it is certain to cause two different patterns of activity among the touch receptors.
evidence: This is based on common experience.

claim: Recent studies suggest that the perceptual space for odors may have rather few dimensions.
source: Beyond arguments by analogy, some recent studies of human olfaction suggest that the perceptual space for odors may have rather few dimensions.
evidence: This is a general statement about recent research trends.

claim: The dominant axes of perceptual odor space can be related systematically to the physical characteristics of odorous molecules.
source: Furthermore, the dominant axes of this perceptual space can be related systematically to the physical characteristics of odorous molecules (Secundo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Secundo et al., 2014.

claim: Mixtures containing many (>20) diverse odorants tend to smell alike, even if they don't share any molecular components.
source: Another relevant observation is that mixtures containing many (>20) diverse odorants tend to smell alike, even if they don't share any molecular components (Weiss et al., 2012), a phenomenon that has been termed 'olfactory white', in analogy to the 'white' percept associated with a mix of many colored lights.
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2012.

claim: The dimensionality of odor percepts may be around 20 or less.
source: This suggests that the dimensionality of odor percepts may be around 20 or less.
evidence: This is an inference from the olfactory white phenomenon.

claim: Mice are readily trained to distinguish odors, even closely related mixtures.
source: Mice are readily trained to distinguish odors, even closely related mixtures.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mouse behavior.

claim: Mice offer an opportunity to stimulate receptor neurons directly by optogenetic activation of the olfactory bulb.
source: More importantly, they offer an opportunity to stimulate the receptor neurons directly, by optogenetic activation of the olfactory bulb (Spors et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spors et al., 2012.

claim: Using optogenetics, arbitrary activation patterns of different olfactory receptor types can be driven by shining patterned light onto the glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
source: In a suitably engineered animal one could drive arbitrary activation patterns of the different olfactory receptor types by shining patterned light onto the glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a proposal for a future experimental approach.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation allows patterns of stimulation that may not ever occur with natural odorants.
source: Also, this method allows patterns of stimulation that may not ever occur with natural odorants; one could then test if the perceptual space differs from receptor space, and is shaped to the ecology of real odors.
evidence: This is speculation about the capabilities of the proposed optogenetic approach.

claim: The olfactory bulb surface can be thought of as a retina for the smell system.
source: In a way, one can think of the olfactory bulb surface as a retina for the smell system.
evidence: This is an analogy proposed by the author.

claim: Olfactory objects produce spatio-temporal patterns on the olfactory bulb surface.
source: Olfactory objects produce spatio-temporal patterns on this surface, and the downstream neural circuits are busy identifying, discriminating, or learning those spatio-temporal patterns.
evidence: This is knowledge about olfactory processing.

claim: The number of dimensions in human pattern vision is much lower than the number of receptors on the retina.
source: It is clear already that the number of dimensions is much lower than the number of receptors on the retina.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vision.

claim: Pairs of visual images can have very different effects on the retina but look the same to human subjects.
source: One can make pairs of visual images that have very different effects on the retina, but look the same to human subjects (Freeman and Simoncelli, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Freeman and Simoncelli, 2011.

claim: A systematic approach to measuring dimensionality of pattern vision is beginning to yield results.
source: And a systematic approach to measuring dimensionality of pattern vision is beginning to yield results (JD Victor, personal communication).
evidence: Based on personal communication with JD Victor.

claim: Pursuing the analogy of smell to pattern vision will be more fruitful than the analogy to color vision.
source: Based on these developments, I suggest that pursuing the analogy of smell to pattern vision will be more fruitful than the analogy to color vision.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: Determining the dimensionality of the space of odor percepts is a precondition to estimating the number of distinct percepts.
source: Regardless of approach though, determining the dimensionality of the space of odor percepts is a precondition to estimating the number of distinct percepts.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The recognition that color space is three-dimensional has had enormous impact in science, art, and technology.
source: The recognition that color space is three-dimensional has had enormous impact in science, art, and technology, as anyone reading this on a color monitor will confirm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the impact of color science.

claim: The search for a basis set for odors has fascinated scientists, engineers, and perfumers for some time.
source: The search for a similar basis set for odors has fascinated scientists, engineers, and perfumers for some time (Gilbert, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilbert, 2008.

claim: Even proving that a low-dimensional basis for odors does not exist would be a major advance.
source: Even proving that a low-dimensional basis does not exist would be a major advance.
evidence: This is an opinion about the value of future research.
